chapter: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
title: Amos Giliad, the toothless trombone virtuoso, and King Oliver selling clams
summary: Dickenson tells of a ragged trombonist in Harrisburg who played an exercise book flawlessly without teeth, and of seeing King Oliver selling clams in Savannah.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: You mentioned earlier a man named Amos Giliad(?).

Oh yeah! I was with Zack Whyte's band, and we went to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. And we were at some hotel there, some third-class hotel or fourth-class hotel or something... You know, we didn't have no money hardly, just scuffling, you know. And here comes this guy, and he was real raggedy, you know. We had a trombone player named Stump Brady. Stump, incidentally, was one of the best lead trombone players. He was really great, and I hope he still can play...

Anyhow, he brought this guy around to the room. And they had one of those Auburn(?) books. It's a big thing. It's a book that you learn in, but it's got all the...all of the trombone things, all the exercises and things that a trombone does. And this guy took Stumpy's horn, and played everything in tempo, all the whole thing, just like triple tones, double tones and everything -- and didn't have no

teeth. He didn't have no teeth. He played without any teeth. He didn't have none of them put in there. He just played, and played everything -- the triple tongue and the double tonguing, the whole bit. And he played them in tempo. That's the greatest trombone player, you know, as far as technique is concerned... I've never seen anybody like that, you know, to read that stuff just like that, you know, and run all through it. They told me he was with a circus band years ago; I think it was James P. Lowry. Have you ever heard of that?

I think he was with him years ago. Amos Giliad(?). He's a man to be remembered that no one knows. He was a street cleaner when he died. Just like King Oliver was selling clams or something on the street. You know? That's a damn shame. It's a shame. These guys should be remembered, because they are great musicians. And you know King Oliver was a great musician. He was one of the great firsts!

Sure! Sure. I seen him down in Savannah, Georgia, I think. Savannah, I think that's where he was at, where I seen him. I was down there with the Blanche Calloway band. He was selling clams or something on the
street. What a great... What a fall for a grand old man like that. You know?
It's strange when you think of it. And he wasn't even that old. I mean, it seemed that way then, but he...
Did Lester ever mention him? Because he worked with him briefly.
I don't remember. I don't remember Lester speaking of him, but it's a possibility.
